subtype: Approach: rushing to finish before the deadline [Pitfall]
passage: Darshan carried his science model into class in a carton this morning, and before he reached his desk the roof slid off and the walls folded like a wet paper bag. Yesterday he had told me he would start after dinner, and he only found the glue at ten at night. He glued the walls wet and went to bed. The glue had not set. He looked at the heap on his desk and said nothing. I don't know if he was angrier with himself or with the glue. I helped pick up the pieces. - Suraj

qa.q: When did Darshan start building the model?
qa.a: He started after dinner the night before, and found the glue at ten at night.

qa.q: What might Darshan have been feeling as he looked at the heap on his desk?
qa.a: Upset and embarrassed, possibly angry with himself, though Suraj cannot tell which.

qa.q: What could Darshan do next time with a deadline, and why?
qa.a: He could start earlier and leave time for the glue to dry, so the model has set before it has to be carried.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the collapse?
qa.a: Suraj is sympathetic and helps pick up the pieces, without knowing exactly what Darshan felt.

grounding: A boy leaves his science model until the night before and glues it wet, and it falls apart in the morning.

subtype: Approach: following a routine of daily watering [Action]
passage:
"Sarika, you're up before me?" said Wasim, rubbing his eyes at the balcony door.
"Watering." She poked a finger into the tin of tulsi. "Still damp. This one can wait." She moved to the marigold tin. "Dry on top. This one gets a mug."
"Why touch the soil every day? Just pour."
"Amma says roots drown if you pour without checking." She tipped the mug slowly. "Two tins, five minutes, then school."
"Fine, fine. Save me a marigold for my shirt pocket."
"They're not for pockets yet." She smiled and picked up her bag.

qa.q: What does Sarika do to check whether a plant needs water?
qa.a: She pokes a finger into the soil.

qa.q: What is Sarika feeling about her plants as she waters them?
qa.a: Caring and content, since she takes her time and smiles as she talks about them.

qa.q: What could Sarika do if she oversleeps one morning, and why?
qa.a: She could ask Wasim to check the soil or water in the evening, so the plants do not go dry.

qa.q: How does Wasim see Sarika's morning routine?
qa.a: Wasim is sleepy and a little amused, teasing her but also asking for a marigold, which shows some interest.

grounding: A girl waters tulsi and marigold each morning before school and checks the soil with a finger first.

subtype: Approach: finding out what each plant needs [Thinking]
passage: Note from Nilesh at the plant nursery. A boy of about ten, Ojas, came in on Saturday and asked what each of his two seedlings needs. I told him chilli wants plenty of sun and mint does better in the shade. He had forgotten his notebook, so he wrote it on his palm. "So chilli by the window and mint next to the wall," he said. I nodded. On Tuesday he came back with a photo of both pots in their places and asked if that was right. It was. - Nilesh

qa.q: Where did Ojas write down what he learned?
qa.a: He wrote it on his palm.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he came back with the photo on Tuesday?
qa.a: Eager and a little unsure whether he was right, but proud enough to show his work.

qa.q: What else could Ojas do to check the plants get the right light, and why?
qa.a: He could watch the pots over several days and move them if the leaves look pale or burnt, because plants show what they need.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see Ojas's return visit?
qa.a: Nilesh is pleased and encouraging, since Nilesh confirms it was right and notes the boy's interest.

grounding: A boy asks a nursery worker what each plant needs and places his pots by the window and the wall accordingly.

passage: Mother had gone to her sister's for a week and left Saurabh in charge of the seedlings on the balcony. Saurabh was thrilled. Morning: a full mug on each pot. After lunch: another. At dusk: another. "More water, faster growth," he told the seedlings. On the fifth day the leaves went yellow and floppy and the soil smelled sour. He rang his neighbour, Preeti Aunty, who tipped a pot and showed him the soft brown roots. "Too much love," she said gently. Half the seedlings were beyond saving, and Saurabh could not look at the empty pots.

qa.q: How often a day did Saurabh water the seedlings?
qa.a: He watered them three times a day: morning, after lunch and at dusk.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when the seedlings' leaves went yellow?
qa.a: Worried and puzzled, since he had tried so hard and things had got worse.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do next time, and why?
qa.a: He could touch the soil first and water only when it feels dry, because roots need air as well as water.

qa.q: How does Preeti Aunty see Saurabh's mistake?
qa.a: Preeti Aunty is kind about it, calling it too much love, and sees eagerness rather than carelessness.

grounding: A child waters seedlings several times a day, thinking more means faster growth, and the roots rot.

passage: Every Sunday after breakfast, Ganga knelt by the bean pot on the balcony with a plastic ruler and a pencil. She measured from the soil to the tip and wrote in her notebook, along with the weather: 6 Jul, 9 cm, dry. 13 Jul, 12 cm, cloudy. 20 Jul, 19 cm, rain on Thursday. "That's a big jump," said her neighbour Alka, peeping through the railing. Ganga turned back a page. "It rained the week before too." She underlined both rainy weeks in blue. The pattern sat there on the page, plain as anything.

qa.q: When did Ganga measure the bean plant?
qa.a: She measured it every Sunday after breakfast.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she saw the pattern on the page?
qa.a: Pleased and curious, since her notes showed something she could not have seen by looking.

qa.q: What else could Ganga record to be more sure of the pattern, and why?
qa.a: She could note how much water and sunshine the plant gets, so rain can be told apart from other changes.

qa.q: How might Alka see Ganga's notebook?
qa.a: Alka is probably impressed, since Alka noticed the big jump and watched Ganga check back through the pages.

grounding: A girl measures a bean plant every Sunday, records the height, and notices it grows fastest after rain.

subtype: Approach: figuring out why the plant is dying [Thinking]
passage: In the school garden club, Francis stared at the brown tips on his chilli plant. "Shalini Ma'am, is it dying?" "You tell me. What could cause brown tips?" Francis counted on his fingers. "Maybe it's thirsty. Maybe sunburnt. Or bugs." He pushed a finger into the soil: damp. "Not water." He looked up: the pot sat in shade after noon. "Not sun." Then he crouched and turned over each leaf. Along the stem ran a line of tiny ants. "Pests!" He brushed them off with a twig and set the pot on a saucer of water. Shalini Ma'am nodded.

qa.q: What did Francis find on the stem?
qa.a: He found a line of tiny ants.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he found the ants?
qa.a: Excited and relieved, since checking each cause in turn had led him to the answer.

qa.q: What could Francis do to keep the ants away, and why?
qa.a: He could keep the pot on a saucer of water and check the stem daily, because ants cannot easily cross water.

qa.q: How does Shalini Ma'am see Francis's method?
qa.a: Shalini Ma'am approves, as her nod shows, since Francis found the cause by reasoning himself.

grounding: A boy asks why a plant is failing, checks water, sun and pests in turn, and finds ants on the stem.

subtype: Approach: making a small compost from kitchen waste [Action]
passage: Sunday, three weeks on. Today the compost pot smells like earth, not peels. Nani Gargi and I dug in: dark, crumbly soil! We mixed a handful into each pot of tomatoes and roses. We began with only kitchen peels, tea leaves and dry leaves from the lane, and Nani said, "Keep turning it, and do not peek every day." I am glad I listened. No fertiliser bought. Nani says the pots will tell us in a week whether it worked. I'll measure the tomato plant on Sundays. - Hansa

qa.q: What went into the compost pot at the start?
qa.a: It began with kitchen peels, tea leaves and dry leaves from the lane.

qa.q: How does Hansa feel now that the compost is ready?
qa.a: Pleased and a little proud, glad to have listened to Nani and pleased to see dark soil.

qa.q: What else could Hansa do with the compost, and why?
qa.a: Hansa could share some with neighbours or use it on other pots, since the peels would otherwise be thrown away.

qa.q: How might Nani Gargi see the finished compost?
qa.a: Nani Gargi is probably proud that Hansa listened and waited, since Nani Gargi taught patience.

grounding: A child makes compost from kitchen waste and dry leaves with a grandmother's help, and uses the dark soil on the plants.

passage: Gautam planted a sunflower seed in the pot beside our stairs on Monday. On Thursday morning I found him kneeling there with his fingers deep in the soil. "Just checking if it's growing," he said. He lifted the seed out, and I saw a thin white thread coming from it, so small. He set it back, pressed the soil down and looked pleased. The next week nothing came up. Gautam dug again and found the seed brown and soft. He looked at it for a long time and said, "I should have waited." I couldn't tell if he was sad or just surprised. - Deepika

qa.q: How many days after planting did Gautam dig up the seed?
qa.a: Gautam dug up the seed on Thursday morning, after planting it on Monday.

qa.q: What might Gautam have been feeling when he found the brown seed?
qa.a: Sad and regretful, though Deepika could not tell whether he was sad or just surprised.

qa.q: What could Gautam do instead of digging while he waits, and why?
qa.a: He could water gently and mark days on a calendar, or grow a second seed in a clear cup to watch, so he can look without disturbing it.

qa.q: How does Deepika see what happened to Gautam's seed?
qa.a: Deepika is sympathetic and cannot tell what Gautam felt, but notes how long he looked at the seed.

grounding: A boy digs up a seed after three days to check on it, kills the tiny root and learns that some things need patient waiting.

subtype: Approach: moving the pots after the leaves burn [Revision]
passage: Garden club note, Tejas Sir. Meenal's rose plant had crisp brown leaves after three hot afternoons. She touched a leaf and said, "It's the sun after lunch." She dragged the pot under the neem tree, where the sun comes only in the morning. Then she gathered dry leaves and spread them over the soil. "Like a blanket, so the water stays." I asked nothing and only watched. A week later, new red leaves were opening on the stem. She showed them to me without a word, and stood with her hands behind her back, smiling. - Tejas Sir

qa.q: Where did Meenal move the rose pot?
qa.a: She moved it under the neem tree, where the sun comes only in the morning.

qa.q: What was Meenal thinking when she touched the crisp leaf?
qa.a: She was worried about the plant and guessed the afternoon sun was the cause.

qa.q: What else could Meenal do to protect the plant on very hot days, and why?
qa.a: She could water early in the morning or use a light cloth for shade, so the plant loses less water in the heat.

qa.q: How does Tejas Sir see Meenal's response?
qa.a: Tejas Sir watches without stepping in and seems pleased, since Meenal found and fixed the problem herself.

grounding: A girl whose rose leaves burn in the afternoon heat moves the pot to partial shade and mulches the soil with dry leaves.

subtype: Approach: sharing the work with a sibling [Action]
passage: Akash and Jomon shared the balcony garden, and for a month they argued. "You never water!" "You never weed!" Then Akash hung a chart on the wall with two columns. Jomon: water each morning. Akash: weeds and dead leaves each evening. Each ticked their own box with a marker on a string. When exams began, the chart kept the plants alive even on nights when neither wanted to look up from the books, because each could see the other's ticks and did their part. Mummy said the tomatoes looked better than they had all holidays.

qa.q: Which job did Jomon take on the chart?
qa.a: Jomon took watering each morning.

qa.q: What were the brothers feeling before the chart, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Annoyed and resentful, since each said the other never did the work.

qa.q: What could the brothers do if one of them is ill, and why?
qa.a: They could swap jobs for a few days and note it on the chart, so the plants are still cared for and neither feels cheated.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the chart and the tomatoes?
qa.a: Mummy seems pleased, since the tomatoes looked better than during the holidays and the arguing had stopped.

grounding: Two brothers share garden jobs on a wall chart so neither feels the other does less and the plants survive exams.
